session.title: Minorities, the Common Citizen and the End of Postponement

speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Manages the Steering Committee election, regulates the continuing Objectives Resolution debate, rules on Jayakar's attempt to add observations after withdrawing his amendment and schedules completion for 22 January.

speakers.name: Rajkumar Chakravarty
speakers.positionSummary: Asks when Steering Committee candidates may withdraw.

speakers.name: K. Madhava Menon
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that the Assembly has already granted the requested delay and should now pass the Objectives Resolution rather than reward continued absence.

speakers.name: B. Das
speakers.stance: Supports Resolution · appeals to Muslim League
speakers.positionSummary: Supports the Resolution while repeatedly appealing to Muslim League colleagues to enter the Assembly and state their differences inside the constitutional process.

speakers.name: Devendranath Samanta
speakers.positionSummary: Grounds constitution-making in popular sacrifice, welfare of the masses, minority safeguards and confidence in a broadly representative Assembly.

speakers.name: Jerome D'Souza
speakers.stance: Supports Resolution · liberty and cultural pluralism
speakers.positionSummary: Defends the democratic creed while warning against excessive state regimentation and against assimilating minorities into a false cultural homogeneity.

speakers.name: H. J. Khandekar
speakers.positionSummary: Supports minority safeguards but demands numerical representation and concrete protection for historically oppressed communities, including people criminalised by birth under colonial law.

speakers.name: R. V. Dhulekar
speakers.positionSummary: Reads the Resolution's core commitments into the record, defends proceeding despite absent parties and argues that the Assembly's authority flows from India's freedom struggle rather than a British gift.

speakers.name: Deshbandhu Gupta
speakers.positionSummary: Questions whether Dhulekar is reading from a manuscript.

speakers.name: H. C. Mookherjee
speakers.stance: Supports Resolution · civic and religious rights
speakers.positionSummary: Supports the Resolution as a minority representative and stresses equal civic, political and religious rights without cultural erasure.

speakers.name: P. R. Thakur
speakers.positionSummary: Asks how long debate on the Resolution will continue.

speakers.name: Balkrishna Sharma
speakers.positionSummary: Asks whether any member may move closure of the debate.

speakers.name: H. V. Pataskar
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that India's divisions make a guiding declaration necessary and warns that sectional charters must not obscure a constitutional charter for the common citizen.

speakers.name: S. H. Prater
speakers.stance: Supports Resolution · compromise and minority protection
speakers.positionSummary: Withdraws earlier support for postponement, defends autonomous provinces within a Union and treats minority protection and negotiated consent as central to unity.

speakers.name: M. R. Jayakar
speakers.positionSummary: Says the Assembly granted the postponement he sought and therefore withdraws his amendment, while attempting to place additional considerations before the House.

speakers.name: Govind Ballabh Pant
speakers.positionSummary: Objects that Jayakar cannot use withdrawal of his amendment to introduce a fresh proposal or reopen debate.

speakers.name: Unnamed Assembly Voice
speakers.positionSummary: Asks whether Jayakar is making a new proposal.

speakers.name: P. S. Deshmukh
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that Jayakar should be allowed to finish explaining his withdrawal so long as he does not move a new amendment.

speakers.name: R. K. Sidhwa
speakers.positionSummary: Warns that permitting new suggestions would require reopening debate so other members can answer them.

speakers.name: C. M. Poonacha
speakers.positionSummary: Defends the Assembly's competence, insists sovereignty belongs to people in British India and the princely States alike, and asks members to think beyond the present generation.

speakers.name: Vishwambhar Dayal Tripathi
speakers.positionSummary: Supports popular sovereignty and justice but presses for socialist institutional guarantees and an explicit declaration that the Constituent Assembly itself is sovereign.

speakers.name: K. Santhanam
speakers.positionSummary: Asks whether the Budget will come before the House on 22 January.

interventions.summary: The President announces thirteen valid candidates for eleven Steering Committee seats and explains that, unless withdrawals reduce the field, election will use proportional representation by single transferable vote later that day.
With Nehru not yet present for another listed item, the Chair directs the House to continue debate on the Objectives Resolution.
Rajkumar Chakravarty asks the deadline for withdrawing a Steering Committee candidature.
The Chair says candidature may be withdrawn any time before voting begins at 3 p.m. and then calls K. Madhava Menon to resume the Resolution debate.

Madhava Menon argues that an objectives declaration is normal and necessary for a constituent body. Since the Assembly already waited until January as Jayakar requested, continued delay would reward absence rather than widen participation.

B. Das supports the Resolution but focuses on the Muslim League's continued absence, appealing to former colleagues to enter the House, state their case and pursue independence through the shared constitutional forum.

Devendranath Samanta connects the Assembly to popular suffering and sacrifice, expresses confidence in its members and argues that the Resolution provides a principled guide for framing a Constitution directed to the welfare of the whole country.

Samanta points to justice, equality and safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas. He argues that political security depends not only on seat counts but also on public goodwill and cooperation across communities.
He says Jayakar's postponement amendment no longer needs to be pressed, links independence to ending exploitation and closes by supporting unanimous adoption of the Resolution.
The Chair announces that Somnath Lahiri and Lakshminarayan Sahu have withdrawn, leaving eleven candidates. The remaining eleven are declared elected without an afternoon poll.

Jerome D'Souza treats the Resolution as a public democratic profession and warns that rapid national development can tempt the State toward force, regimentation and excessive central power at the expense of individual liberty.

D'Souza warns that minorities can be injured not only by explicit discrimination but by well-intentioned pressure toward cultural or religious homogeneity. He argues for national unity that preserves distinct community life.

H. J. Khandekar supports the Resolution's safeguards but speaks from the experience of the Scheduled Castes, pressing for representation proportionate to population and describing continuing social oppression.

Khandekar asks that people classified from birth as 'criminal tribes' receive constitutional protection, voices fear for Scheduled Castes in proposed groupings and insists token representation will not satisfy politically awakened communities.

R. V. Dhulekar supports the Resolution and reads its principal commitments—independence, Union, popular authority, justice, freedoms, territorial integrity and contribution to world peace—into his argument.
Deshbandhu Gupta asks whether a member may read from a manuscript.
The President replies that Dhulekar appears to be using extensive notes rather than simply reading a manuscript.

Dhulekar argues that the Resolution protects backward classes and minorities, rejects further delay for absent State or Muslim League representatives and attacks separate electorates as a source of communal division.

He rejects the claim that the Assembly is merely a British creation, roots its authority in the Indian freedom struggle and ends by promising equality and justice to communities that fear majority rule.

H. C. Mookherjee supports the Resolution so that small religious and social minorities are visibly associated with it. He stresses fundamental civic and political rights, religious freedom and continued space for distinct religious life.
P. R. Thakur asks how long debate on the Resolution will continue.
The President says he cannot yet say when debate will finish.
Balkrishna Sharma asks whether any member can move closure.
The Chair confirms that any member may move closure.

H. V. Pataskar argues that India's religious, territorial, social and economic divisions make a common statement of objectives necessary. He warns that the scramble for sectional charters must not obscure a constitutional charter that protects every ordinary citizen.

S. H. Prater says postponement is no longer justified. He supports provincial autonomy within an Indian Union and argues that durable unity depends on strong minority protections and a negotiating spirit rather than bare majority power.
The Chair calls M. R. Jayakar to make a statement about his amendment.

Jayakar says the Assembly effectively accepted his request to wait until 20 January. Because that delay was granted, he considers himself bound not to press his amendment, though he begins to offer additional considerations.
Govind Ballabh Pant objects that Jayakar has already used his opportunity and should not turn withdrawal of the amendment into a new proposal or renewed debate.
An unidentified member asks whether Jayakar is putting forward a new proposal.
The President rules that no new proposal may be made and says Jayakar was called only to state his position while withdrawing the amendment.
Jayakar argues that withdrawal should still allow him to explain the considerations behind it.
P. S. Deshmukh argues that Jayakar should be allowed to complete his explanatory statement so long as he is not moving a fresh amendment.
R. K. Sidhwa counters that any new suggestions would need answers from other members and would reopen the debate unfairly.
The Chair closes the procedural dispute, concludes that Jayakar has exhausted the opportunity and puts withdrawal to the House. The Assembly grants leave and the amendment is withdrawn.

C. M. Poonacha supports the Resolution as compatible with the Cabinet Mission framework, argues that sovereignty belongs to people in the princely States as well as British India and urges the Assembly to frame a Constitution for future generations, not only the present one.

Vishwambhar Dayal Tripathi supports the Resolution but warns that familiar constitutional ideals can be emptied by those who control state power. He presses for socialist guarantees so justice and popular authority cannot be interpreted against ordinary people.

Tripathi argues that a body proclaiming an Independent Sovereign Republic should itself declare sovereign authority derived from the people and rejects the idea that the Assembly owes its existence simply to the Cabinet Mission statement.
The President says the House has debated the Resolution for several days and intends to complete it on 22 January. He also notes another Nehru resolution still awaits consideration.
K. Santhanam asks whether the Budget will come up the next day.
The Chair says the Budget may appear on the agenda and the Assembly adjourns until 11 a.m. on 22 January 1947.
